title: Are You the One Who Runs 'Maanava Nesan'?
translation_notes: Fresh T1 translation made directly from the pinned Tamil after complete P0/source review. No pre-existing English translation was consulted.
The repeated chapter heading in the first extraction unit is represented only as title metadata.

paragraphs: Jinnah and Jawaharlal Nehru continued to correspond. They were entirely about the Muslim community. In connection with the Muslims' demands, the Congress Party did not accept the conditions contained in a letter Jinnah wrote on 9 October 1938. Opposition between Jinnah and the Congress took deep root.

The Muslims of Tamil Nadu lived on friendly terms with the leaders of the Justice Party. At celebrations held in honour of the Prophet Muhammad in Tamil Nadu, Periyar, Anna, Alagiri, Chittarasu and others took part and spoke. It would be no exaggeration to say that this relationship helped forge the strong bond that would continue between the Dravidian movement and the Muslim League.

When Gandhiji and Janab Jinnah met for talks, Gandhiji looked at Jinnah in astonishment and asked, "Are you the Jinnah who, in 1915, stood as the representative of both Hindus and Muslims?" Janab Jinnah replied, "Nationalism is not anyone's private property."

Gandhiji, Subhas Bose and Jinnah together held talks on 18 June 1938. Jinnah presented a plan containing fourteen conditions. It was not accepted. That year, the distance between the Congress and the Muslim League increased. In direct contrast, the closeness between the Dravidian movement and the League in Tamil Nadu grew.

That year, while Hindu-Muslim conflict continued in the north and the anti-Hindi struggle in Tamil Nadu, internal turmoil and foreign invasion seemed to outdo one another in neighbouring China. Across Europe, the dark clouds of war gathered and rumbled. The conditions for war had taken shape. Disturbances in Burma that year claimed many lives and caused extensive damage to property.

Though that year had begun amid an atmosphere of war, the following year, 1939, Rajaji's ministry came to an end. An interim ministry was formed. That ministry removed the compulsory-Hindi law. We may therefore regard 1939 itself as the year of our first-stage victory in the language struggle.

It was now that a major split began to develop within the Indian National Congress as well. At the Congress session held at Tripuri, Subhas Bose stood for the presidency again. Jawaharlal Nehru, who had returned from abroad, tried to dissuade him, but Subhas would not listen. Gandhiji too did not want Subhas to contest a second time. Subhas Chandra Bose argued: why should he not remain Congress president just as Jawaharlal had done for two successive years? In the end, despite Gandhiji's opposition, Subhas Chandra Bose contested and won.

Gandhiji wanted a Muslim to become president of the Congress. He had Abul Kalam Azad in mind. When Subhas insisted on contesting, Azad withdrew. Gandhiji fielded Pattabhi Sitaramayya against Subhas. Sitaramayya lost so decisively that Mahatma Gandhi, deeply pained, had to say that Pattabhi's defeat was his own defeat. Following that defeat, Gandhiji, Azad, Patel and Rajendra Prasad resigned from the Congress Working Committee.

They refused to accept Subhas's leadership. Seeing the problem grow and grow, Subhas Bose resigned his post. Rajendra Prasad, who enjoyed Gandhiji's affection, was then elected president of the Congress.

Meanwhile, Subhas Chandra Bose declared that a non-cooperation movement should be launched in India against the British government, already troubled by the prospect of war in Europe. Gandhiji's argument was that taking advantage of the opportunity to oppose England while it was caught in crisis would violate the principles of satyagraha.

Having cast aside the responsibility of leadership, Subhas Bose now set out to revolt against the Congress. He thundered against the resolutions passed by the Congress Party in Bombay. Across the country his sympathizers began speaking against the Congress resolution. The Congress immediately took action against him. Disciplinary action was taken, barring Subhas, one of its great leaders, from contesting for a Congress post for three years.

It was an occasion on which the party organization was held to be greater than any individual. Yet it also became an event that proclaimed to the world the importance of Gandhiji's place within that organization.

Nehru took great pains to keep Gandhiji and Subhas together. It was for that reason that, even when the great leaders resigned from the Congress Working Committee, he did not resign. Pandit Nehru wrote to Gandhiji, "It would be good to accept Subhas as president." But Gandhiji did not agree to this till the very end.

Subhas Bose, elected president of the Tripuri Congress, had a fever of 105 degrees. They carried him in and seated him at the conference. I remember very well reading newspaper reports at the time which said, "Even in that pitiable condition, neither of the two groups gave up its principles or its stubbornness."

On 14 November came Jawaharlal Nehru's fiftieth birthday. The poet-songbird Sarojini Devi sent Nehru a message of greeting: "Your first thirty years have already won a foremost place in the history of India."

Unable to bring Gandhi and Subhas together, a disillusioned Nehru accepted China's invitation and went there as an envoy of the Congress. Soon after he arrived, the world war began, and within ten days he returned to India.

It was in this very year, 1939, that M. N. Roy started the Radical Democratic Party. Subhas Bose's Forward Bloc too was marching against the Congress Party in another direction. The Communist Party was making strong preparations to penetrate many parts of the country.

One man engaged in such efforts wanted to meet me while I was still a schoolboy. He must have imagined that a person called Karunanidhi would be roughly his own age and build. I went and stood before him—a thin fifteen-year-old youth.
He looked at me doubtfully and asked, "Are you Karunanidhi, the one who runs 'Maanava Nesan'?"
'Maanava Nesan' was a handwritten journal that I ran. Even now, students in many places run handwritten journals.

Once, poet Bharathidasan read a handwritten journal given to him by a student and wrote this review: "If believing that the country will advance through the spinning wheel is madness, this handwritten magazine is just as mad."

No one has said that the country will advance in one stroke simply because students run handwritten journals. Little drops make a great flood. A country is made up of many people. The future of that country belongs to its students.

It is my belief that handwritten journals give students a good opportunity to refine and polish their thoughts. Major magazines do not accept what one writes in youth. I would say that the practice one gains from a handwritten journal amply equips one to write for such magazines.

But there is one thing. Everyone turns out something like a Pongal special issue under the name of a handwritten journal. The handwritten journals I ran at school could be read by only one person at a time.

The journal I ran came out twice a month. Each issue had eight pages. There were no fewer than fifty copies. Only a few friends and I would sit and copy all fifty by hand. We collected only the cost of the demy paper. The labour and the articles were free!

'Maanava Nesan' continued in this way for seven or eight months. Writing out fifty copies by hand and distributing them like this was difficult. When I began to wonder what else could be done, that was when 'Murasoli' was born. Not as a weekly or a monthly. As leaflet issues!
Only four months before 'Murasoli' began, the bespectacled man in the khadi shirt had met me.

He asked me: "All the students must be united and arrayed to raise their voices for Freedom, Peace and Equality. A Students' Federation has been formed as an organizing camp for that purpose. You must serve as its organizer and enroll members in the Tiruvarur school."
Though he wore a khadi shirt and spoke proudly of the national leaders, it became clear that he was not a Congressman. I did not know then that the man operating behind the scenes was a Communist.

How many emotions could the words Freedom – Peace – Equality kindle in the heart of a fifteen-year-old youth! And so I became the organizer of the Students' Federation. Two hundred members were enrolled. Congress students too joined, believing the Federation to be Congress-affiliated. Of those two hundred, one hundred were unaffiliated students who belonged to no party.
The current of the Federation seemed ready to sweep us along with it. I kept worrying that we had put a foot in without knowing the depth.
